questions.q: Which of the following findings would immediately raise concern for systemic infection rather than erythema toxicum neonatorum in a pustular neonatal eruption?
opts: Vesicles and pustules appearing at 48 hours of life in a full-term infant
A similar eruption in a preterm infant weighing 2000 g
Predominant eosinophils on Wright-Giemsa smear cytology
Sparing of the palms and soles with blotchy facial involvement
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum neonatorum is a disease of healthy infants over 2500 g, and a pustular eruption in a preterm or low-birth-weight infant should always prompt evaluation for systemic infection. The birth-weight threshold is a critical epidemiological feature distinguishing benign ETN from potentially serious neonatal infections.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Transient Neonatal Pustular and Vesicular Eruptions
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A TINY PREMATURE BABY (under 2500g weight) sits in the castle NEONATAL ICU wearing a RED ALERT SIREN around their neck—ETN cannot touch them, so ANY pustule = INFECTION HUNT begins immediately.

questions.q: A 3-day-old infant with large, irregular, non-membranous midline scalp defects and terminal transverse limb defects (syndactyly, shortened digits) is evaluated. On imaging, a skull ossification defect is noted with prominently dilated scalp veins. Which genetic etiology and classification group best describes this presentation?
opts: Group 1 ACC; sporadic mutation in BMS1 gene
Group 2 ACC (Adams-Oliver Syndrome); autosomal dominant mutations in ARHGAP31, RBPJ, NOTCH1, or DLL4
Group 3 ACC; autosomal recessive inheritance with epidermal nevi
Group 4 ACC; X-linked dominant mutation affecting vascular development
questions.exp: Adams-Oliver Syndrome (Group 2 ACC) is characterized by large, irregular, non-membranous scalp defects overlying skull ossification defects with dilated scalp veins, combined with the defining feature of terminal transverse limb defects (syndactyly, shortened digits). This syndrome follows autosomal dominant inheritance (mutations in ARHGAP31, RBPJ, NOTCH1, DLL4) or autosomal recessive patterns (DOCK6, EOGT mutations), distinguishing it from the solitary membranous scalp lesions of Group 1.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: ADAMS-OLIVER = SCALP DEFECT + SHORTENED LIMBS, imagine OLIVER TWIST's TWISTED SHORT HANDS reaching up to touch a HOLE IN HIS SKULL (Group 2).

questions.q: A collodion baby is born at 35 weeks gestation and develops severe hypernatremic dehydration and temperature instability within the first 24 hours of life. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains these life-threatening complications?
opts: Hypothalamic dysfunction impairing thermoregulation and ADH secretion
Profound impairment of the skin barrier resulting in markedly increased transepidermal water loss
Sepsis-induced disseminated intravascular coagulation affecting vascular integrity
Congenital renal tubular acidosis reducing sodium reabsorption capacity
questions.exp: The collodion membrane consists of a markedly thickened, compact, orthokeratotic stratum corneum that acts as a severely impaired skin barrier, leading to profoundly increased transepidermal water loss (TEWL). This massive fluid loss drives hypernatremic dehydration and impairs the infant's ability to maintain core temperature, resulting in temperature instability—hallmark complications of collodion baby that account for high perinatal morbidity and mortality. The skin barrier dysfunction is primary; hypothalamic, renal, and sepsis-related mechanisms are secondary consequences rather than the fundamental pathophysiology.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine the castle's CELLOPHANE MOAT (collodion = cellophane) has GIANT LEAKS, with WATER GUSHING OUT endlessly—the castle floods (hypernatremia from water loss) and the heating system fails (temperature instability from barrier breakdown).

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with non-pruritic, scaly erythematous plaques on her cheeks and upper chest that worsened after a beach holiday. Histopathology shows vacuolar alteration of the basal layer with apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte bodies), superficial lymphocytic infiltrate, dermal edema, and prominent mucin deposition. There is NO hyperkeratosis, basement membrane thickening, or scarring. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
opts: Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE)
Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE)
Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE)
Lupus tumidus
questions.exp: SCLE is characterized by photosensitive, non-scarring lesions with interface dermatitis featuring vacuolar basal damage, Civatte bodies, superficial lymphocytic infiltrate, and prominent dermal mucin deposition. The conspicuous absence of hyperkeratosis, basement membrane thickening, and scarring distinguishes SCLE from DLE, which shows these features prominently.
questions.memory_hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture SCLE as a SUPERFICIAL (shallow lymphocytes), STICKY (mucin deposition), SCAR-LESS party on sun-exposed skin—while DLE builds DEEP underground bunkers (deep infiltrate, hyperkeratosis, scarring) in the castle basement.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man is prescribed Saturated Solution of Potassium Iodide (SSKI) for sporotrichosis. When counseling him on administration, which statement is correct?
opts: Each drop of SSKI contains 100 mg of potassium iodide
SSKI should be taken undiluted for optimal absorption
The solution should be discarded if it turns yellow-brown in color
A standard dropper dispenses 40 drops per mL, so 1 drop equals 25 mg
questions.exp: SSKI contains 1,000 mg (1 g) of KI per mL, with a standard calibrated dropper dispensing 20 drops per mL, meaning 1 drop equals 0.05 mL or 50 mg. The solution has a bitter taste and causes gastrointestinal irritation, so drops must be diluted in water, milk, or orange juice. A yellow-brown discoloration indicates iodine oxidation and degradation, necessitating discard of the solution.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A YELLOW-BROWN THRONE (oxidized iodine) appears in the SSKI castle—THROW IT OUT! Remember: 20 DROPS per mL, so each GOLDEN DROP = 50 mg (not 100), and DILUTE before swallowing or the bitter guards will irritate your GI kingdom.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a symmetrical, coppery-red maculopapular rash involving his palms and soles. He reports a history of a painless ulcer on his genitalia that appeared 8 weeks ago and has since healed. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains the current clinical presentation?
opts: Local tissue invasion by Treponema pallidum at the site of primary chancre
Massive hematogenous dissemination (spirochetemia) with generalized tissue reaction to T. pallidum
Immune complex deposition limited to palmar and plantar tissues
Reactivation of dormant spirochetes in regional lymph nodes
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis develops 6-8 weeks after the primary chancre and results from massive hematogenous dissemination (spirochetemia) with generalized tissue reaction to T. pallidum throughout the body. This systemic infection produces the characteristic symmetrical, non-pruritic, coppery-red rash that famously involves the palms and soles, distinguishing it from the localized pathology of primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with known pulmonary tuberculosis presents with chronic, progressive erythematous plaques on her cheeks that show a characteristic "apple-jelly" appearance on diascopy. Histopathology reveals tuberculoid granulomas with caseation. Which cutaneous manifestation is she most likely suffering from?
opts: Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis
Tuberculous gumma
Lupus vulgaris
Acute miliary tuberculosis
questions.exp: Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous TB in adults and presents with soft, reddish-brown plaques showing a pathognomonic "apple-jelly" color on diascopy. It is characterized by simultaneous progression and involution with potential for significant tissue destruction. The combination of the adult age, chronic progressive nature, and the distinctive diascopic finding is diagnostic.

questions.q: Regarding the pathogenesis of Kawasaki disease, which statement most accurately reflects our current understanding of the disease's initiating mechanism and molecular target?
opts: Kawasaki is primarily an autoantibody-mediated disease targeting desmoglein adhesion molecules, similar to pemphigus

The causative agent remains unknown; it is not a primary autoimmune disease, and no specific host autoantigen is currently identified, though oligoclonal IgA antibodies suggest an intracellular viral pathogen
Staphylococcal exotoxins directly cleave specific elastin proteins in the coronary arterial wall
The disease is exclusively caused by group A Streptococcus that has been isolated from all affected patients on bacterial culture
questions.exp: Kawasaki disease is fundamentally different from autoimmune bullous diseases: there is no known host autoantigen or specific target receptor. Current evidence suggests a ubiquitous, unidentified infectious agent (possibly a respiratory virus) triggers aberrant immune activation in genetically susceptible hosts. Oligoclonal IgA from KD patients bind to cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in ciliated epithelium, suggesting an intracellular pathogen, and cultures remain sterile.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A MYSTERIOUS CASTLE (unknown agent) with no NAME PLATE on the door—inside, GHOSTS (IgA antibodies) chase INVISIBLE VIRAL SHADOWS in the BRONCHIAL towers, but the CORONARY MOAT below is flooded with inflammation.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with painful subcutaneous nodules on her shins consistent with erythema nodosum. Which mechanism best explains potassium iodide's therapeutic efficacy in this condition?
opts: Direct fungicidal activity against causative organisms
Induction of mast cell heparin release to suppress delayed hypersensitivity reactions
Inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis reducing inflammation
Bactericidal effect through generation of reactive oxygen species
questions.exp: Potassium iodide lacks direct antimicrobial or fungicidal activity but is highly effective for erythema nodosum through host immune modulation. In hypersensitivity disorders like erythema nodosum, KI induces mast cells to release large quantities of heparin, which subsequently suppresses delayed hypersensitivity reactions within affected subcutaneous tissue.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a MAST CELL castle guard releasing a GIANT HEPARIN ROPE to tie down and suppress the angry immune reactions storming the SHIN FORTRESS at the EN Estate.

questions.q: A 9-year-old boy presents with progressive nail dystrophy, reticulate hyperpigmentation on his neck and chest, and oral leukoplakia. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the DKC1 gene at Xq28. Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms underlies this condition?
opts: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of melanocytes via pathogenic IgG antibodies
Mutations in telomere maintenance genes leading to critically shortened telomeres and premature cellular senescence
HLA-associated immune complex deposition in the basement membrane zone
Defective T-regulatory cell function causing loss of immune tolerance to epithelial antigens
questions.exp: Dyskeratosis congenita is fundamentally a disorder of telomere biology, not autoimmunity. Mutations in genes encoding telomerase complex components (such as DKC1/dyskerin) or shelterin proteins cause critically shortened telomeres, leading to premature cellular senescence and apoptosis, particularly affecting rapidly dividing hematopoietic and epithelial cells. This is NOT an immune-mediated disease, and routine autoimmune serology is non-applicable.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy with EBV infection develops symmetric, highly pruritic vesicular lesions on his hands and feet, with Type B morphology featuring coalescing edematous plaques. Importantly, liver function tests remain normal. Compared to classic Gianotti-Crosti disease, which histological feature is most prominently increased in this non-HBV variant?
opts: Hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging within the stratum corneum
Marked epidermal spongiosis and substantially intensified dermal inflammatory infiltrates
Subcutaneous fat necrosis with granulomatous reaction
Basal cell layer vacuolization with colloid body formation
questions.exp: The papulovesicular acrolocated syndrome (non-HBV associated) demonstrates histologically identical patterns to classic Gianotti's disease, but with substantially MORE MARKED epidermal spongiosis and dermal inflammatory infiltrates due to the vesicular nature of the lesions. This heightened inflammation correlates clinically with the pronounced pruritus and prolonged course seen in this variant.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the NON-HBV castle wing, a MASSIVE SPONGE (spongiosis) SOAKS UP INFLAMMATORY LYMPHOCYTES like a tidal wave—vesicular means MORE swelling, MORE inflammation, MORE drama than boring classic HBV papules.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with symmetric, pink-to-red-brown papules on the face, buttocks, and extensor surfaces of the extremities. Systemic examination reveals hepatomegaly and mildly elevated liver enzymes. Which viral antigen is most likely responsible for this classic presentation?
opts: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) surface antigen
Hepatitis B surface antigen (Australia antigen)
Coxsackievirus A16 capsid antigen
Parvovirus B19 structural protein
questions.exp: Classic Gianotti-Crosti syndrome, the original form described in the 1950s, is specifically triggered by Hepatitis B surface antigen (Australia antigen), with historical epidemics linked to subtypes ayw and adr. The defining feature is the coexistence of acute anicteric hepatitis with the characteristic papular eruption. Modern non-HBV variants are more common post-vaccination, but this patient's hepatic involvement points to HBV etiology.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture the AUSTRALIAN OUTBACK (Australia antigen) with a HEPATITIS-STRICKEN KANGAROO's LIVER glowing red in a child's BUTTOCK-SHAPED bouncy castle—only classic HBV-Gianotti pairs hepatitis with the rash.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy of Japanese descent presents with severe blistering sunburn after 15 minutes of outdoor play. He has progressive poikiloderma and early signs of neurological decline. Genetic testing reveals mutations in the XPA gene. Which of the following best describes the primary molecular defect in this patient?
opts: Loss of DNA helicase function within the TFIIH transcription-repair complex
Defective DNA damage verification in the nucleotide excision repair pathway
Impaired translesion DNA polymerase activity across UV-induced photoproducts
Mutations in the DDB2 gene encoding damage-binding protein 2
questions.exp: XP-A (complementation group A) results from mutations in the XPA gene encoding the XPA protein, which is responsible for DNA damage verification/recognition in the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway. This is the most common subtype in Japan and presents with severe sunburn sensitivity and neurodegeneration (De Sanctis-Cacchione Syndrome when complete loss-of-function occurs). XPB encodes a helicase (not XPA), translesion polymerase defects characterize XP-Variant, and DDB2 mutations define XP-E.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A JAPANESE WARRIOR (XP-A, most common in Japan) stands at the GATE VERIFICATION booth (damage verification), checking all damage reports entering the NER castle fortress—if the guard is broken, NO damage alerts get through, and UV photoproducts pile up like unchecked invaders.

questions.q: A 2-day-old male neonate is admitted to the NICU encased in a taut, transparent, parchment-like membrane resembling plastic wrap. Over the next 3 weeks, the membrane dries and peels off in sheets, revealing large, dark-brown, plate-like scales arranged in a bark-like mosaic pattern with severe ectropion and scarring alopecia. Which gene mutation is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
opts: ALOXE3 encoding lipoxygenase
TGM1 encoding transglutaminase-1
NIPAL4 encoding ichthyin
CYP4F22 involved in vitamin D metabolism
questions.exp: The clinical picture of a collodion baby evolving into lamellar ichthyosis (LI) with characteristic dark-brown plate-like scales, severe ectropion, eclabium, and scarring alopecia is most consistent with TGM1 gene mutations, which encode transglutaminase-1—an enzyme critical for cornified cell envelope formation. ALOXE3 mutations cause congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE) with prominent erythroderma rather than plate-like scales. TGM1 accounts for the majority of lamellar ichthyosis cases and this inheritance pattern represents approximately 80–90% of collodion baby presentations.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a GLUE GUN (TGM1/transglutaminase) in the castle's outer wall CEMENTING PLATE-LIKE STONES into a BARK MOSAIC—when the glue factory breaks down, the wall becomes thick, rigid, and peels like bark.

questions.q: Among patients seeking cosmetic surgery and dermatologic procedures, what is the estimated prevalence of Body Dysmorphic Disorder compared to the general population?
opts: 1–2.5% in cosmetic-seeking patients versus 5–10% in general population
7–15% in cosmetic-seeking patients versus 1–2.5% in general population
3–5% in cosmetic-seeking patients versus 0.5–1% in general population
10–20% in cosmetic-seeking patients versus 7–15% in general population
questions.exp: The note explicitly states BDD affects 1–2.5% of the general population but 7–15% of patients seeking cosmetic procedures, making BDD screening essential in aesthetic dermatology. This significantly elevated prevalence in the cosmetic-seeking population reflects how BDD patients typically present to dermatologists and surgeons rather than psychiatrists due to lack of insight.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman undergoes dermal filler injection for nasolabial fold enhancement. Shortly after injection, she develops sudden excruciating pain, arborizing blanching, and duskiness along the nasal distribution. What is the immediate next step in management?
opts: Apply topical antibiotic ointment and observe for 24 hours
Stop the injection immediately and flood the area with hyaluronidase along the affected artery course
Refer to ophthalmology for retrobulbar hyaluronidase injection
Administer IV hydrocortisone and systemic antihistamines
questions.exp: Vascular occlusion from inadvertent intravascular filler injection is a medical emergency. The injection must be stopped immediately, and for hyaluronic acid fillers, hyaluronidase (10–30 Units per 2×2 cm area, up to 1500 Units total) should be flooded along the affected artery course. Warm compresses, vigorous massage, topical nitroglycerin paste, and oral aspirin support vasodilation and circulation restoration.

questions.q: During a cosmetic procedure, a patient suddenly develops stridor, wheezing, hypotension, urticaria, and angioedema within minutes of local anesthetic administration. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
opts: Immediate administration of systemic IV hydrocortisone and IV antihistamines
Adrenaline 1:1000 injected intramuscularly into the mid-anterolateral thigh, with patient placed supine or in Trendelenburg position and high-flow oxygen
Rapid infusion of normal saline IV fluids alone while monitoring for resolution
Oral antihistamines and observation in a semi-upright position
questions.exp: Anaphylaxis is an IgE-mediated life-threatening emergency requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) 1:1000 (0.2–0.5 mL) as the treatment of choice. The patient must be positioned supine or in Trendelenburg with elevated legs, given high-flow oxygen, and IV fluids established. Systemic antihistamines and corticosteroids are second-line agents to prevent protracted symptoms but never replace adrenaline.

questions.q: A patient with subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) undergoes direct immunofluorescence of a lesional skin biopsy. Which pattern of immunoglobulin deposition is suggested to be more specific for SCLE?
opts: Granular pattern of IgG along the basement membrane zone
Dust-like particle pattern of IgG around epidermal basal keratinocytes
Linear pattern of IgG and IgM along the dermal-epidermal junction
Diffuse cytoplasmic pattern of IgA in the superficial dermis
questions.exp: The 'dust-like particle' pattern of IgG deposition around basal keratinocytes is suggested to be more specific for SCLE and reflects in vivo bound Ro/SS-A autoantibodies. This distinctive immunofluorescence pattern occurs in approximately 60% of SCLE patients and helps differentiate it from other forms of lupus.
questions.memory_hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine DUST MOTES glowing around the BASAL BRICK wall of the castle when sunlight (Ro/SS-A) shines through—SCLE's sparkly signature that other lupus types lack.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with a round, punched-out defect on the scalp vertex covered by a thin, translucent epithelial membrane. Examination reveals a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair surrounding the lesion. What is the most likely histological finding and the clinical significance of the hair collar sign?
opts: Absence of epidermis with intact dermis; hair collar sign is pathognomonic for underlying neural tube defect
Full-thickness skin necrosis with dermal inflammation; hair collar sign indicates favorable prognosis
Hyperkeratosis with follicular acanthosis; hair collar sign is a benign epidermal variant
Subcutaneous adipose tissue hypertrophy; hair collar sign represents compensatory hair growth
questions.exp: Membranous aplasia cutis congenita (ACC) classically presents as a round/oval punched-out defect with absent epidermis and skin appendages, covered by a thin epithelial membrane. The pathognomonic 'hair collar sign'—a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair—is a critical clinical marker that should alert clinicians to investigate for underlying neural tube defects, as it suggests incomplete closure of embryonic ectodermal fusion lines.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SCALP VERTEX with a PUNCHED-OUT HOLE (like a ticket booth), ringed by a DARK HAIR COLLAR—the collar is TIED TO THE SPINAL CORD UPSTAIRS (neural tube defect in the castle tower).

questions.q: Histologically, lichen striatus demonstrates a T-cell-mediated immune response. Which subset of T lymphocytes predominates in the inflammatory infiltrate attacking mutated keratinocytes?
opts: CD4+ helper T cells
CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes
Regulatory T cells (Tregs)
Gamma-delta T cells
questions.exp: CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes are the primary effector cells in lichen striatus, found scattered or clustered around necrotic keratinocytes, indicating direct attack on the aberrant mosaic epidermal clone. This cell-mediated immunity is triggered when a precipitant breaks immune tolerance to the somatic mutation-derived clone. 🏰 Palace: Picture CD8 EXECUTIONERS (CD8+) as CASTLE GUARDS with SWORDS (cytotoxic granules) stabbing MUTANT TRAITOR BRICKS (necrotic keratinocytes) in the palace wall—they HUNT and KILL the aberrant cells.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with secondary syphilis presents with patchy, non-scarring hair loss at the scalp margins, eyebrows, and beard region. Additionally, she has deeply fissured papules at the angles of her mouth and nasolabial folds. Which of the following best describes the specific dermatological findings?
opts: Follicular syphilids with pseudopelade alopecia
Moth-eaten alopecia and split papules
Condylomata lata with scarring alopecia
Papulosquamous lesions with diffuse telogen effluvium
questions.exp: The clinical presentation describes two pathognomonic lesions of secondary syphilis: "moth-eaten" alopecia (patchy, non-scarring hair loss at scalp margins, beard, and eyebrows) and split papules (deeply fissured papules at the angles of the mouth and nasolabial folds). These distinctive findings are characteristic features that aid in diagnosis of secondary syphilis.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a MOTH (patchy hair loss) eating the EDGES of the castle, while a SPLIT apple (fissured papule) divides the MOUTH CORNER—secondary syphilis's signature hallway defacement.

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant presents with a 6-day history of high spiking fever and only two mucocutaneous criteria consistent with Kawasaki disease. Which of the following statements best explains why this clinical presentation is particularly concerning?
opts: Incomplete Kawasaki in infants <6 months carries the highest risk for coronary artery aneurysms because diagnostic delay is common with atypical presentation
Infants have inherently defective IgA responses that prevent effective complement activation against viral pathogens
The incomplete variant is actually milder than classic Kawasaki and requires no urgent intervention
Infants younger than 6 months cannot develop coronary complications regardless of treatment timing
questions.exp: Incomplete Kawasaki disease (≥5 days fever with only 2–3 classic features) most commonly affects infants <6 months and paradoxically places them at highest risk for life-threatening coronary artery aneurysms because the atypical presentation frequently delays diagnosis and treatment with IVIg. The diagnostic trap requires supportive labs (ESR ≥40, CRP ≥3.0) or echocardiographic confirmation.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a tiny BABY (6 months) in the castle nursery with only 2 out of 5 royal CRESTS on their clothing, yet the GOLDEN CROWN (coronary arteries) behind them is CRUMBLING fastest—small body, BIG danger from delay.

questions.q: A full-term neonate presents with scattered erythematous macules and firm 1–3 mm pustules with an irregular surrounding erythematous halo on the trunk and face at 36 hours of life. Smear cytology shows predominant eosinophils and occasional neutrophils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection
Erythema toxicum neonatorum
Congenital varicella
Neonatal candidiasis
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN) is an extremely common benign condition affecting 48–72% of full-term newborns, classically beginning 24–48 hours after delivery with the pathognomonic 'flea-bitten' appearance (central papule/pustule surrounded by irregular sea of erythema) and profoundly sparing palms and soles. Smear cytology showing predominant sterile eosinophils with occasional neutrophils is characteristic and rules out infectious etiologies.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Transient Neonatal Pustular and Vesicular Eruptions
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a FLEABITE (ETN classic sign) on a NEWBORN'S CHEEK at 36 HOURS, with a SWARM OF EOSINOPHILS (yellow-staining bugs) crawling out of a SMEAR SLIDE in the castle moat—sterile, benign, vanishing like ghosts by tomorrow.

questions.q: A 28-year-old female presents to your dermatology clinic requesting laser treatment for mild facial erythema that she believes makes her 'completely disfigured.' She admits to spending 2–3 hours daily checking mirrors and wearing heavy makeup to camouflage the redness. She has already consulted with three other dermatologists and two plastic surgeons over the past 6 months. On mental status examination, she lacks insight into the severity of her concern. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Proceed with laser therapy as the redness may objectively improve her appearance and boost self-confidence
Refuse the cosmetic procedure and refer for psychiatric evaluation, as her presentation is consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder
Perform a brief trial of topical corticosteroids first, then reassess her expectations in 2 weeks before deciding on laser treatment
Prescribe fluoxetine 20 mg daily and schedule laser treatment in 4 weeks once mood improves
questions.exp: This patient exhibits classic red flags for BDD: excessive mirror checking, camouflage behavior, multiple doctor shopping, and lack of insight despite minimal objective defect. Cosmetic procedures are contraindicated in BDD as they rarely satisfy patients and often exacerbate distress, increasing litigation risk. Psychiatric referral with CBT and SSRIs (at higher doses) is first-line treatment, not cosmetic intervention.

questions.q: A 2-year-old with xeroderma pigmentosum develops multiple basal cell carcinomas, squamous cell carcinomas, and melanoma by age 10. Which of the following molecular events directly explains the extraordinarily high cancer risk in this condition?
opts: Defective mismatch repair leading to microsatellite instability and colorectal cancer predisposition
Impaired nucleotide excision repair causing massive accumulation of UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts
Loss of p53 tumor suppressor function with absent DNA checkpoint control
Homozygous BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations resulting in defective homologous recombination
questions.exp: Xeroderma pigmentosum is fundamentally a disorder of nucleotide excision repair (NER), the primary pathway responsible for removing UV-induced DNA photoproducts including cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts. When NER is defective (as in XP-A through XP-G), these lesions accumulate unchecked, leading to genomic instability, massive mutation burden, and catastrophic early-onset carcinogenesis. Mismatch repair defects, p53 mutations, and BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations are associated with different hereditary cancer syndromes but not XP.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a CASTLE LIBRARY (the nucleus) where UV RAYS punch through windows creating DIMERS (stacked Lego blocks—CPDs and 6-4 photoproducts) piling up on every shelf; the NER REPAIR WORKERS are paralyzed/absent, so the blocks accumulate into CANCER TOWERS that collapse catastrophically before age 10.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl presents with a linear eruption following the lines of Blaschko on her left arm that appeared 3 weeks ago. The lesions are unilateral and have not responded to emollients. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lichen striatus
Linear psoriasis
Verruca vulgaris
Atopic dermatitis
questions.exp: Lichen striatus is a benign, self-limiting linear inflammatory dermatosis that characteristically follows the lines of Blaschko and predominantly affects children aged 5–15 years. The unilateral linear distribution along embryonic cell migration pathways is pathognomonic for this condition. 🏰 Palace: Imagine a STRIPED TIGER (LS) walking along an ANCIENT BLASCHKO CASTLE WALL during its CHILDHOOD JOURNEY—only one side of the wall is marked, following the exact path of medieval construction lines.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the forearm following a minor puncture wound 4 weeks ago. Regional lymph nodes are matted and enlarged. Which form of cutaneous tuberculosis is most consistent with this clinical presentation?
opts: Scrofuloderma
Tuberculous chancre
Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis
Lupus vulgaris
questions.exp: Tuberculous chancre (primary inoculation TB) occurs in individuals never previously exposed to TB and follows minor trauma such as puncture wounds or tattoos. It presents as a painless, indurated ulcer accompanied by matted regional lymphadenopathy, analogous to the Ghon complex in pulmonary TB. The acute onset following trauma and the characteristic matted lymphadenopathy distinguish this from other forms.

questions.q: A 12-year-old girl presents with the classic triad of dyskeratosis congenita. Her mother is asymptomatic despite carrying the same DKC1 mutation. Which inheritance pattern and mechanism best explains the mother's clinical protection?
opts: Autosomal recessive inheritance with the mother being a heterozygous carrier
X-linked recessive inheritance with the mother's protective skewed X-inactivation expressing the normal allele
Autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance in females
Mitochondrial inheritance with maternal heteroplasmy conferring clinical resistance
questions.exp: Classic X-linked recessive dyskeratosis congenita (Zinsser-Cole-Engman syndrome) results from DKC1 mutations at Xq28. Female carriers are typically asymptomatic due to skewed X-inactivation, which preferentially silences the mutant allele and allows expression of the normal telomerase-encoding copy on the unaffected X chromosome. This explains why affected males (male-to-female ratio ~3:1) present with disease while carrier females remain protected.

questions.q: At what gestational age can Treponema pallidum first cross the placental barrier and infect the fetus in congenital syphilis?
opts: 4-6 weeks of gestation
9-10 weeks of gestation
14-16 weeks of gestation
20-22 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: Treponema pallidum can cross the placental barrier as early as 9 to 10 weeks of gestation, allowing transplacental transmission to occur at any time during pregnancy. This early timing emphasizes the critical importance of antenatal screening and early maternal treatment.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a pregnant woman at 9-10 weeks standing at the PALACE GATES (9-10), watching Treponema spirochetes sneaking ACROSS THE MOAT (placental barrier) like tiny invaders—the earliest they can breach the defenses.

questions.q: A pregnant woman with primary syphilis is not treated before 16-18 weeks of gestation. What is the approximate transmission risk to her fetus?
questions.exp: Transmission risk approaches 70% to 100% in pregnant women with primary or secondary syphilis. This high risk drops to approximately 40% in early latent syphilis and falls to 10% in late latent or tertiary syphilis, reflecting the organism burden and maternal immune stage.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the PRIMARY SYPHILIS chamber, spirochetes SWARM like a massive army—70-100% DEVASTATION across the placental throne room. Secondary joins the siege with equal ferocity.
